newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asians taste for meat seen boosting soybean demand.
newsitem.headline: Asians taste for meat seen boosting soybean demand.

text.p: Asian giants China and India are seen leading the region's growing demand for soybean -- an important ingredient of animal feeds -- as more Asians consume meat, industry sources said on Monday.
"Asia is a huge demand-growing point," Hemant Bhatt, general manager of trading firm Louis Dreyfus Asia Pte Ltd told Reuters at the sidelines of a soybean conference in Jakarta.

"The big swing factors are China, and to a lesser degree India followed by Indonesia and Thailand," he said. "(South) Korea, Japan and Taiwan are important for the origin from which they will buy rather than how much."

He said China's soybean production was projected by his company at 16.3 million tonnes in 1997/98 (October/September), against 12.6 million tonnes in 1996/97, adding that the expected rise in output could see a decline in imports.
"Soybean imports will continue, but at a lower pace due to the higher production," he told the conference.

He said demand for soybean was also growing in India, where 65 percent of the population were meat-eaters compared with 45 percent 10 years ago. "The economy is growing and people are eating more meat."
Bhatt said India's soybean production was expected at around 4.4 million tonnes in 1997/98, barely changed from the previous year, subject to weather conditions.

"India's crop could be 4.4 million tonnes or a low of 2.1 million tonnes depending on whether it's a normal or abnormal monsoon," he said. Bhatt however added that he felt the crop should come in at no lower than three million tonnes.
He said 40 percent of India's soybean crop had been planted so far, along with 25 percent of the groundnut crop, adding that the monsoon started eight to 10 days late in June.
He said the next round of rains were expected in mid-July and the last batch in August.
"The El Nino has a strong correlation with India," he said of the weather pattern forming in the South Pacific which can cause drought from India to Australia.
Bhatt said that if the El Nino phenomenon takes place, the impact can be seen as early as within two months.
"Currently the crop (soybean) is being planted in China and in India. They need moisture during the growing season," he said.
"The corelation between El Nino and India is more so than China. China has its own weather patterns," he said.

Zenaida Linsangan, purchasing officer at Vitarich Corp of the Philippines, told the conference China was expected to import between 2.5-3.0 million tonnes of soybean meal in 1997, against 1.7 million tonnes last year.
She said China's compound feed production had grown from a mere one million tonnes in 1978 to about 48-50 million tonnes currently.

"Apart from China, the other countries in Asia such as Indonesia, Thailand as well as the Philippines could experience growth in imports," she said. "Overall, there is an estimate of about 8 million tonnes import demand for Asia alone."
